concept.title: Meet Cerberus: A Puppy with Big Drive!
concept.shortdesc: Hi, I'm Cerberus! I'm an energetic and intelligent working dog breed looking for my forever home. Please read through this PDF guide to see if we're a good match!

section.title: Overview
section.p: Cerberus is a 10-month-old German Shepherd–Boxer mix with strong instincts and a clear need for structure. He thrives in a calm, predictable environment and builds deep bonds with the people who guide him. If you enjoy working with intelligent, responsive, and energetic dogs, then Cerberus may be an ideal fit.

section.title: His Journey So Far
section.p: Cerberus started life in a rural setting with lots of open space but little structure. His early training relied more on discipline than reward, and he was later housed in a small hotel room with minimal outlets for energy or stimulation. Despite this, he stayed eager to connect and responded quickly to kindness and routine. When his living situation changed, Cerberus was brought to North Carolina, where he adjusted well in boarding care and showed how resilient and responsive he truly is.

section.title: What He Needs
section.p: Cerberus will thrive in a home that offers:

ul.li: Mental stimulation through play, training, or enrichment
Adults or children over five who respect boundaries
Limited time alone; he does best with a consistent daily care plan

section.p: He prefers stable households with minimal chaos. As a working breed, Cerberus will thrive in a space with a backyard or even on a farm!

section.note: He is not suited for homes with cats, chaotic energy, or owners seeking a low-energy pet.

section.p: We’ve created several tools to help you through the adoption process. Here are some tools:

section.title: Ready to Adopt?
section.p: If Cerberus sounds like a good fit for your home or foster program, please explore the full adoption package, and contact Christina Mayr, the foster coordinator. She’ll follow up shortly to begin the conversation!

concept.title: Cerberus Match Guide
concept.shortdesc: This guide outlines Cerberus’s care needs, temperament, and compatibility to help determine if you and Cerberus are a good match. A strong match ensures long-term success for both dog and caregiver.

section.title: Ideal Home Environment
section.p: Cerberus thrives in calm, structured environments. He benefits from consistent routines and companionship throughout the day. A house with a secure yard works best. Cerberus is not suited to apartment living.

ul.li: Human presence during most of the day

section.title: Energy Compatibility
section.p: Cerberus brings enthusiasm and a strong working drive. He needs regular movement, stimulation, and shared purpose. Daily walks, play, and short training sessions help him feel settled and engaged.

ul.li: Toys and games that challenge his mind

section.title: Experience Level
section.p: Cerberus responds to steady, confident leadership. With guidance, he adapts well and enjoys learning. Experienced handlers and new adopters who commit to structure and support can succeed with him.

section.title: Household Compatibility
section.p: Cerberus does best in adult-only homes or with children over 5 years old. He prefers environments free from overstimulation. His high prey drive makes cat-free homes ideal. He may live well with a calm, balanced dog after a careful introduction.

section.title: Feeding and Food Habits
section.p: Cerberus eats well and responds to food as a training tool. He enjoys a steady routine and a balanced diet.

ul.li: Two meals daily of dry kibble
Likes yogurt, peanut butter, broths, and watermelon
Fast eater and drinker (slow feeder recommended)
Begs at the table but is not fed from it

section.title: Temperament and Activity
section.p: Cerberus is alert, affectionate, and playful. He builds bonds quickly and shows joy when given shared tasks.

ul.li: Needs structured walks and mental games
Enjoys treat balls, squeaky toys, beach balls
Supervision recommended during soft toy play

section.title: Socialization
section.p: Cerberus connects deeply and thrives in homes with structure. He values routine, activity, and companionship.

ul.li: Trained to give hugs, doesn’t jump up
Pack-oriented; enjoys daycare and dog companions

section.title: Training Needs
section.p: Cerberus shows strong potential and benefits from structured, positive reinforcement.

ul.li: Currently in formal training with Lydia Register (AAS, CPDT-KA)
High prey drive (squirrels, rabbits, small dogs)

section.note: Lydia Register will offer discounted training sessions to Cerberus's future adopter.
section.p: Training success depends on:

ul.li: Remote or hybrid worker: Excellent match for consistent engagement
Active adult or couple: Good fit for shared activity and bonding
Retiree with routine: Works well if structured and attentive
High-traffic or chaotic home: Not a good match
Confined living space (i.e., apartment): Not a good match

section.title: Summary
section.p: Cerberus is energetic, trainable, and full of heart. He builds trust with presence, structure, and mutual respect. Cerberus is a great companion who will grow alongside a dedicated owner.
section.note: For adoption or foster inquires, please reach out to Christina Mayr.

reference.title: Common Housing Questions
reference.shortdesc: This reference answers the most common questions about preparing your home for Cerberus.

section.title: Q: Do I need a house with a yard to adopt Cerberus?
section.p: A: Yes, Cerberus is best suited to houses with backyards to allow him to meet his daily activity needs. He needs at least 60 minutes of combined walking and play every day, i.e., two 30-minute walks a day. If you have a yard, ensure it is fully fenced with no gaps or weak spots.

section.title: Q: How long can Cerberus be left alone?
section.p: A: Cerberus does best when someone is home for part of the day. If you work full-time, arrange a midday potty break with a dog walker, neighbor, or doggy daycare. He should not be left alone for more than 4–5 hours without a break.

section.title: Q: Does Cerberus need a crate?
section.p: A: Cerberus can tolerate crates and sleep in crates for extended periods with appropriate encouragement. A soft-sided crate or a quiet “safe area” can be used for short rest periods, but a gated room or playpen is often a better option.

section.title: Q: How should I set up my home before Cerberus arrives?
section.p: A: Prepare a calm space with his bed, bowls, and toys ready. Remove anything he might chew (cords, shoes, small objects). Secure trash, cleaning supplies, and medications so they are out of reach.

section.title: Q: Can Cerberus live with cats or other small pets?
section.p: A: Cerberus is not compatible with cats and has a strong prey drive. Small pets must have fully secure enclosures and be closely supervised if they are in the same home.

section.title: Q: Can Cerberus live with another dog?
section.p: A: Cerberus may do well with a calm, balanced dog after slow, careful introductions. Success depends on the other dog’s temperament and the adopter’s ability to manage the process.

section.title: Q: What if my home situation is different from these examples?
section.p: A: Every home is unique. If you have questions about your specific setup, please reach out to the foster team. For foster team contact information, please see the Foster Contact Sheet Internal reference for foster team and volunteers. Lists key contacts, their roles, and the best way to reach them for Cerberus’s care and adoption needs.

section.title: Q: What are Cerberus’s exercise needs if I work long hours?
section.p: A: Cerberus needs at least 60 minutes of combined daily exercise. If you work long hours, consider arranging a midday dog walker or daycare. A longer walk or play session before and after work will also help him feel balanced.

section.title: Q: How do I introduce Cerberus to children?
section.p: A: Cerberus does best in adult-only homes or with children over five years old. Always supervise interactions, teach children to respect Cerberus's space, and avoid hugging or rough play. For more information on how to introduce Cerberus to children, contact Lydia Register, Cerberus's trainer, to set up a training session.

section.title: Q: How should I handle visitors coming to my home?
section.p: A: Cerberus can be protective of his space. Keep him leashed or behind a gate during arrivals and reward calm behavior as guests enter. Give him time to adjust at his own pace. For more information on how to introduce Cerberus to visitors, contact Lydia Register, Cerberus's trainer, to set up a training session.

section.title: Q: Can Cerberus handle stairs or open spaces?
section.p: A: Yes, but supervise him around open staircases or elevated spaces. Block access with baby gates if you’re not confident about safety.

section.title: Q: How much time should I plan to spend at home during the first weeks?
section.p: A: Plan to be home as much as possible in the first 1–2 weeks to help Cerberus decompress and learn his routine. Gradually increase time away once he’s more settled.
